opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my doubt came from how reinforcement learning had succeeded before. The famous wins, like Atari, Go, and robotics in simulation, all had two things language didn't seem to have: a clean reward signal and a manageable action space. In Go you win or you lose. In a game you get a score. With language, what's the reward for a paragraph? Whether it's "good" is subjective and depends on context. It's hard to write down as a number.

Then there's the action space. Every token is a choice among tens of thousands of options, and a response might be hundreds or thousands of tokens long. So you're doing credit assignment over a huge combinatorial space with a reward that only arrives at the very end. From the classic RL point of view that looks like a nightmare: high variance, unstable training, very sample-inefficient.

The early experiments in text generation reinforced that. People tried policy gradient methods on things like summarization or dialogue with automatic metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE as the reward. The models learned to game the metric. You'd get outputs that scored higher but read worse, sometimes degenerate, repetitive text. That's reward hacking in its purest form. So my intuition was that supervised learning on good data was the reliable path, and RL was a fragile trick that added noise.

What I underestimated was the role of the pretrained model. Once you start from a strong language model, you're no longer exploring randomly in that huge space. The model already puts most of its probability on reasonable continuations. RL isn't teaching it language from scratch. It's reshaping preferences within a space that's already pretty good. That changes the exploration problem completely.

The second thing was reward. Learned reward models from human preferences, and later verifiable rewards in domains like math and code, gave us signals that were much more meaningful than BLEU. In math, the answer is either right or wrong, so you get back that clean, Go-like signal. Combine a strong prior with a reward that actually tracks what you care about, and RL starts to work, sometimes surprisingly well. You even see behaviors emerge, like the model learning to check its own work or backtrack, that nobody explicitly supervised.

So I don't think my original doubt was unreasonable given the evidence then. I was looking at RL as the thing doing all the work, when the real story is that pretraining does most of it and RL is the last step that aligns and sharpens. Once I saw it that way, the success made a lot more sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my skepticism came from the gap between what reinforcement learning needs and what language actually gives you.

RL works beautifully when the reward is clean and the environment is dense. Go, Atari, robotics simulators: you take an action, the world responds, you get a score. Language isn't like that. A sentence is a sequence of maybe thirty discrete decisions, and the reward, if you can even define one, arrives at the very end. So you're asking the model to figure out which of those thirty tokens was responsible for the output being good or bad. That credit assignment problem seemed brutal to me.

And then there was the reward itself. For a game, winning is winning. For text, what does "good" mean? Early on, people were optimizing against things like BLEU or ROUGE, and those are proxies that fall apart the moment you push on them. The model learns to game the metric. You'd get outputs that scored higher but read worse. I remember thinking, this is just reward hacking with extra steps, and we're going to spend all our effort fighting the policy rather than improving it.

The third thing was variance. Policy gradient methods in a vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens, with sparse reward, meant the gradient signal was incredibly noisy. You'd see training runs that looked like random walks. The supervised baseline was stable, cheap, and you could reason about it. RL felt like paying a lot of compute to get something fragile.

So my instinct was that the bottleneck wasn't optimization at all. It was that we didn't have a reliable way to say what we wanted. And until you solve that, better optimization just helps you arrive at the wrong destination faster.

What changed my mind, and we can get into this, was realizing the reward model could be learned from human comparisons rather than specified by hand. Once the reward was something a model could represent, a lot of my objections became engineering problems rather than fundamental ones. But I was genuinely wrong about how far that would go.

astra-6.text: My initial doubt was about the reward signal. With language, there isn’t usually one clearly correct answer. A response can be fluent but unhelpful, or accurate but poorly explained. So what exactly do you reward? I worried that the model would learn to satisfy whatever scoring rule we gave it without actually becoming better at communicating. And because you’re making a long sequence of word choices, it’s difficult to know which choices deserve credit for a good result. That made reinforcement learning seem like a much less natural fit than learning directly from examples of good text.

sol-6.1.text: My initial concern was the reward signal. With natural language, there are many perfectly good ways to say something, and it’s hard to turn that into a clear score. If the reward captures only part of what we want, the model might learn to get a higher score without actually producing better language. So I wasn’t sure reinforcement learning would improve the things we really cared about.
